case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a federal court sitting in diversity must enforce Delaware’s state-law affidavit-of-merit (AOM) prerequisite for filing/maintaining a medical-negligence action, or instead treat it as displaced by the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Delaware’s medical-negligence Affidavit of Merit (AOM) statute/requirement (a state-law pre-suit or early-suit certification requirement that a qualified expert supports the claim).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Berk argues that Delaware’s AOM requirement is a state procedural screen that conflicts with (and is therefore superseded by) the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure governing pleading, commencement of actions, and sanctions for improper filings (e.g., Rules 3, 8, 9, 11, 12, and 26). Under the Rules Enabling Act and Hanna/Shady Grove framework, he contends the Federal Rules supply the exclusive federal standard for what must be filed to initiate and pursue a negligence claim in federal court; requiring an AOM adds an extra, non-Federal-Rules hurdle that can lead to dismissal regardless of the adequacy of the federal pleading and thus should not apply in federal diversity litigation.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Choy and Beebe Medical Center argue that Delaware’s AOM requirement is a substantive condition on the right to sue for medical negligence (or, at minimum, an integrated state-law rule designed to define and limit malpractice liability) that must be applied in federal diversity cases under Erie to prevent forum shopping and inequitable administration of the laws. They maintain there is no true ‘direct collision’ with the Federal Rules because those rules govern pleadings, discovery, and litigation conduct, while the AOM statute sets a state-law prerequisite for maintaining a malpractice claim and can operate alongside the Federal Rules. Respondents and supporting amici also emphasize that enforcing the AOM requirement advances key policy interests (deterring non-meritorious claims, controlling costs, and protecting access to care) and aligns with Rule 11’s anti-frivolousness objectives rather than contradicting them.
key_precedents: Shady Grove Orthopedic Associates, P.A. v. Allstate Insurance Co.
Federal Rules of Civil Procedure (commonly invoked in the briefing: Rules 3, 8, 9, 11, 12, 26)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch press the strongest point: that Rules 3, 8, 11, and 12 form a comprehensive federal commencement-and-screening regime, so Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit creates a direct, dismissal-triggering incompatibility. But under Hanna and Burlington Northern we ask whether the Federal Rules, fairly read, answer the same specific question, and Walker v. Armco Steel cautions against treating general pleading/commencement provisions as displacing state-law conditions tied to the viability of a state-created claim. Justice Sotomayor’s narrow reading of Rule 11(a)’s “except when otherwise specifically provided by rule or statute” as limited to federal enactments is plausible, but the text does not say “federal,” and a minimalist course is to avoid manufacturing a collision where the Rules can operate alongside a claim-specific state certification requirement. Reading the Rules to nullify Delaware’s AOM risks enlarging the state cause of action in federal court and reviving Erie forum-shopping concerns without a clear on-point federal directive.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point is that Rules 3, 8, 11, and 12 form a comprehensive federal commencement-and-screening scheme, making Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit an incompatible add-on. But that reads the Rules at too high a level of generality; fairly read, they specify what a complaint must contain and how federal courts police pleadings, not whether a State may define the continued maintenance of a state-created malpractice claim to depend on an expert certification—Walker v. Armco Steel cautions against treating general federal pleading/commencement rules as displacing claim-specific state conditions. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Rule 11(a)’s “except when otherwise specifically provided by rule or statute” matters textually: it undercuts the premise that the Rules are an exhaustive catalog of all legally required certifications, and the text does not say “federal,” so I will not rewrite it to manufacture exclusivity. Finally, Justice Sotomayor’s Shady Grove/Stevens framing does not answer the Rules Enabling Act problem as I see it: construing the Federal Rules to nullify Delaware’s gatekeeping would effectively enlarge the state-law right to sue in federal court, which the Act forbids.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point is that Rules 3, 8, 11, and 12 form a comprehensive federal pleading-and-screening regime, so Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit necessarily conflicts by adding a dismissal-triggering filing prerequisite. But that defines the “same question” at too high a level of generality; as Walker v. Armco Steel teaches, we should not treat general federal filing rules as displacing state law conditions tied to the viability of a state-created claim absent a clear textual command. Chief Justice Roberts’s focus on Rule 11(a)’s “except when otherwise specifically provided by rule or statute” reinforces that the Federal Rules are not written as an exclusive catalog of all filing-time certifications, and the text does not confine “statute” to federal law. Given Erie’s forum-shopping and inequitable-administration concerns, and the Rules Enabling Act risk of effectively enlarging Delaware’s malpractice cause of action if the AOM is nullified, I would continue to read the Federal Rules narrowly enough to avoid a manufactured collision.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh make their best point from Rule 11(a)’s proviso (“except when otherwise specifically provided by rule or statute”), but I remain unconvinced it silently incorporates state-law, dismissal-triggering filing prerequisites into what suffices to commence and maintain a federal civil action under Rules 3 and 8. Walker v. Armco Steel, as Justice Kavanaugh stresses, counsels against manufacturing conflicts when a Federal Rule is not on point; here, however, the Federal Rules are on point as to what must be filed and how sufficiency is policed (Rules 8, 11, 12), and Delaware’s AOM operates at that same procedural moment as an additional mandatory attachment on pain of dismissal. Justice Barrett’s and Justice Thomas’s Rules Enabling Act concern does not alter my view under Justice Stevens’s Shady Grove approach: applying the Federal Rules here regulates process transsubstantively and preserves uniform access to federal court without rewriting Delaware’s substantive negligence standard. Erie’s forum-shopping worry cannot override a valid, applicable Federal Rule, and pragmatically the AOM functions as a procedural gate that falls hardest on resource-constrained plaintiffs.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point is Rule 11(a)’s “except when otherwise specifically provided by rule or statute,” but I still read that proviso in its signature/certification context as coordinating with other federal rule/statute regimes—not as quietly authorizing state-by-state, dismissal-triggering attachments that would redefine what a Rule 8 complaint must include to proceed in federal court. Walker v. Armco Steel (as Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas invoke it) matters insofar as we should avoid inventing conflicts, but Walker turned on Rule 3’s silence about tolling; here Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit operates at the same pleading/filing stage and is enforced by dismissal notwithstanding compliance with Rules 8 and 12’s screening framework, which is a direct operational clash. The Rules Enabling Act concern Justice Thomas raises is real, yet under Justice Stevens’s Shady Grove approach the Federal Rules remain procedural as applied because they regulate the manner of litigating (pleading and sanctions) transsubstantively and do not alter Delaware’s substantive elements of malpractice. Erie’s forum-shopping concerns cannot defeat an on-point Federal Rule, and treating the AOM as merely a “condition on maintaining the claim” risks collapsing the collision inquiry into a labels game that would erode uniform federal procedure.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s (and Justice Kavanaugh’s) best point is Rule 11(a)’s “except when otherwise specifically provided by rule or statute,” but I do not read that proviso as silently incorporating state-law, claim-specific filing add-ons that operate as a mandatory attachment-to-the-complaint requirement on pain of dismissal; in context, it most naturally refers to other governing signature/certification regimes within the federal system. Justice Thomas’s Walker v. Armco Steel analogy is worth taking seriously, yet Walker involved tolling—an issue the Rules did not purport to answer—whereas Delaware’s AOM targets the same procedural moment and function already occupied by Rules 3 and 8 (what must be filed to commence) and Rules 11/12 (how inadequate filings are policed), so the “no collision” framing depends on reading the Federal Rules as oddly indifferent to an extra dismissal trigger. Justice Barrett’s Rules Enabling Act concern does not persuade me on these facts because enforcing the Federal Rules’ transsubstantive pleading/commencement baseline does not alter Delaware’s substantive standard of care or elements; it rejects only a state procedural gatekeeper dictating dismissal mechanics in federal court. Erie’s forum-shopping worries, while real, cannot justify rewriting the scope of on-point Federal Rules, and the better textual/originalist course is to apply the federal scheme as written.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Gorsuch’s best point is that Rules 3, 8, 11, and 12 form a transsubstantive federal pleading/screening package, and a state affidavit-of-merit looks like an added, dismissal-triggering filing prerequisite at the same moment. But under Hanna and Walker, I think that frames the “same question” too broadly: the Federal Rules specify what a complaint must contain and how it is policed, while Delaware’s AOM is better understood as a claim-specific condition on continuing to litigate a state-created malpractice right—something the Rules do not clearly purport to negate. The Chief Justice’s reliance on Rule 11(a)’s “except when otherwise specifically provided by rule or statute” reinforces that the Rules are not textually exclusive of other legally required certifications; even if Justice Sotomayor’s narrower ‘federal-only’ reading is plausible, the absence of a clear collision counsels a Walker-style construction that avoids displacing an integrated state screen and the attendant Erie forum-shopping. Given the institutional and Rules Enabling Act concerns flagged by Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas, I do not see a sufficiently on-point Federal Rule to justify preemption here.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch press the strongest point that Rules 3, 8, 11, and 12 form a comprehensive federal pleading-and-screening regime, so Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit necessarily conflicts by adding a dismissal-triggering filing requirement. But under Hanna as applied in Walker v. Armco Steel, the question is whether the Federal Rules, fairly construed, address this claim-specific condition on maintaining a state-created malpractice action; reading the Rules at that higher level of generality risks manufacturing a collision. Chief Justice Roberts’s textual point about Rule 11(a)’s “except when otherwise specifically provided by rule or statute” reinforces that the Federal Rules are not written as an exclusive catalog of all legally required certifications, and the text does not limit “statute” to federal statutes. Given the Rules Enabling Act concern (echoed by Justice Thomas) that displacement would effectively enlarge the state-law right to sue by stripping Delaware’s built-in gatekeeping, Erie’s anti-forum-shopping and equitable-administration aims properly support applying the AOM in diversity absent a clear, on-point Federal Rule to the contrary.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on Rule 11(a)’s “except when otherwise specifically provided by rule or statute” is the best respondent-side move, but I still read that clause in context as an internal cross-reference to other applicable certification regimes in federal law, not an opening for state-by-state, dismissal-triggering add-ons that redefine what suffices to file and maintain a federal complaint. Walker v. Armco Steel, which Justice Kavanaugh emphasizes, reinforces that we should avoid manufactured conflicts when a Federal Rule is genuinely silent on the operative issue (there, tolling), but here Delaware’s AOM answers the same practical federal question—what must accompany the complaint on pain of dismissal—already governed by Rules 8, 11, and 12, making coexistence illusory rather than harmonious. Justice Barrett’s Rules Enabling Act concern does not persuade me under Justice Stevens’s Shady Grove framework: applying the Federal Rules as written regulates procedure transsubstantively and does not alter Delaware’s substantive negligence elements, while importing the AOM would create uneven access and practical inequity in federal court. Erie’s forum-shopping concerns cannot override an on-point Federal Rule, and pragmatically the federal system has ample tools (Rule 11, Rule 12, case management) to deter meritless claims without importing a resource-sensitive gatekeeper.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under Hanna v. Plumer and Burlington Northern R. Co. v. Woods, the first question is whether a Federal Rule, fairly construed, is sufficiently broad to “directly collide” with Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit prerequisite. Rule 11(a) expressly contemplates additional, non-Rule requirements for filings (“except when otherwise specifically provided by rule or statute”), leaving room for Delaware’s AOM to operate and undermining any claim that Rules 8, 11, or 12 occupy the field. With no direct collision, Erie Railroad Co. v. Tompkins and Hanna’s second step counsel applying Delaware’s AOM as an integrated state-law limitation on maintaining a medical-negligence action, to avoid forum shopping and inequitable administration of the laws. A narrow ruling enforcing the AOM in diversity respects federalism and preserves the Federal Rules without extending them to displace state substantive screening mechanisms absent a clear conflict.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Under Erie Railroad Co. v. Tompkins, a federal court sitting in diversity must apply state substantive law defining the elements and conditions of a state-created medical-negligence cause of action. Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit requirement functions as a substantive condition on maintaining that state claim, and none of the cited Federal Rules (Rules 3, 8, 11, 12, 26) “answers the question in dispute” by purporting to eliminate state-law prerequisites for suit; thus there is no direct collision under Hanna v. Plumer. Even if one could characterize an overlap, displacing Delaware’s AOM regime would risk “abridg[ing], enlarg[ing] or modify[ing]” substantive rights in violation of the Rules Enabling Act, 28 U.S.C. § 2072(b), as emphasized in Justice Stevens’s controlling concurrence in Shady Grove. Applying the AOM requirement also serves Erie’s aims by preventing forum shopping and inequitable administration of the laws between state and federal courts.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Under Erie Railroad Co. v. Tompkins and Hanna v. Plumer, the threshold question is whether any Federal Rule is sufficiently broad to “answer the question” and directly collide with Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit prerequisite. The Federal Rules invoked (Rules 3, 8, 11, 12, 26) regulate pleading, sanctions, and discovery, but they do not purport to displace state-law conditions that define when a medical-negligence claim may be maintained; thus there is no direct collision under Burlington Northern R.R. Co. v. Woods and the Shady Grove framework. Treating the AOM requirement as inapplicable would invite forum shopping and produce inequitable administration by allowing malpractice plaintiffs to evade Delaware’s substantive screening mechanism simply by choosing federal court, contrary to Erie’s core concerns. Enforcing the AOM statute also serves strong practical interests in deterring non-meritorious malpractice suits, a policy choice Delaware is entitled to embed in the contours of its liability regime and that the Rules Enabling Act (28 U.S.C. § 2072(b)) cautions federal procedure should not abridge.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit requirement functions as an extra, front-end filing prerequisite that directly collides with the Federal Rules’ comprehensive scheme for commencing an action and testing the sufficiency and good-faith basis of pleadings (Rules 3, 8, 11, and 12). Under Hanna v. Plumer and the Rules Enabling Act, when a Federal Rule answers the question presented and is a valid “rule[] of practice and procedure,” it governs in diversity unless it abridges a substantive right; an AOM screen chiefly regulates the manner and timing of filing rather than defining the elements of medical negligence. Applying the Shady Grove framework (particularly Justice Stevens’s controlling concurrence), enforcing Delaware’s AOM in federal court would allow a state procedural gatekeeping device to override the Federal Rules and disproportionately bar access for plaintiffs—especially vulnerable litigants—despite the federal safeguards against frivolous claims. Because the Federal Rules provide the operative standards for pleading and sanctions, Delaware’s AOM prerequisite should be treated as displaced in federal diversity litigation.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under Hanna v. Plumer and Justice Stevens’s controlling concurrence in Shady Grove, we first ask whether the Federal Rules “answer the question in dispute”—here, what must be filed to commence and maintain a civil action and the consequences of insufficient pleading. Rules 3 and 8 (commencement and pleading) together with Rules 11 and 12 supply a comprehensive federal scheme for initiating suit and policing nonmeritorious filings; Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit prerequisite imposes an additional, categorical dismissal-triggering filing requirement that directly collides with that scheme. Because those Federal Rules are quintessential “general rules of practice and procedure,” applying them does not violate the Rules Enabling Act, 28 U.S.C. § 2072(b), and the state AOM cannot be enforced in federal court even if it advances state policy goals. Erie’s forum-shopping concerns cannot override a valid Federal Rule that governs the point in dispute.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit prerequisite answers the same question the Federal Rules answer—what must be filed and when to commence and maintain a civil action—so it creates an impermissible additional hurdle in federal court beyond Rules 3 and 8’s commencement-and-pleading scheme, enforced through Rules 11 and 12. Under Hanna v. Plumer and Shady Grove (Stevens, J., controlling), when a valid Federal Rule “answers the question in dispute,” it governs unless it violates the Rules Enabling Act, 28 U.S.C. § 2072(b), by abridging substantive rights; these transsubstantive Rules regulate litigation procedure rather than define malpractice liability. Allowing a state to condition access to a federal forum on an extra filing requirement would undermine the uniform operation of the Federal Rules and invite state-by-state displacement of federal procedural law. Because the relevant Federal Rules are valid “rules of practice and procedure” within § 2072(a), the conflicting state AOM requirement must give way in diversity cases.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under Hanna v. Plumer, a Federal Rule displaces state law only when there is a “direct collision,” and the Federal Rules should not be read so broadly as to create avoidable conflicts. Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit requirement can operate alongside Rules 8, 12, and 26 because it functions as a state-law prerequisite to maintaining a medical-negligence claim rather than a competing federal pleading standard, and Rule 11(a) expressly leaves room for additional certification requirements imposed by other law, reinforcing the absence of a direct conflict (see also Burlington N. R.R. v. Woods; Walker v. Armco Steel). Proceeding to Erie, declining to enforce the AOM would invite forum shopping and produce inequitable administration of the laws by allowing plaintiffs to bypass a significant state-law limitation on malpractice suits simply by choosing federal court. Applying the AOM requirement in diversity thus best respects state substantive policy choices while maintaining a workable federal-state balance consistent with the Rules Enabling Act, 28 U.S.C. § 2072.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit requirement functions as a condition on maintaining a state-created medical-negligence cause of action, and the Federal Rules do not clearly “answer the same question” by supplying an exclusive list of prerequisites to sue. Under Hanna v. Plumer and Justice Stevens’s controlling concurrence in Shady Grove, a Federal Rule displaces state law only if there is a direct collision and the Rule, as applied, does not “abridge, enlarge or modify any substantive right” within the meaning of the Rules Enabling Act, 28 U.S.C. § 2072(b). Here the AOM statute is tightly bound up with Delaware’s substantive calibration of malpractice liability and screening of claims; applying a Federal Rule to negate that prerequisite would risk enlarging the state-law right to sue and undermining Erie’s aims of preventing forum shopping and inequitable administration of the laws. Because the Federal Rules (e.g., Rules 3, 8, 11, 12) can operate alongside an expert-certification prerequisite without irreconcilable conflict, the federal court should enforce the AOM requirement in diversity.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit requirement operates as an additional, mandatory filing prerequisite that conditions whether a medical-negligence action may proceed, which directly collides with the Federal Rules’ comprehensive scheme for commencing and testing the sufficiency of civil actions—particularly Rules 3 and 8 (commencement and pleading), and Rules 11 and 12 (certification/sanctions and dismissal standards). Under Hanna v. Plumer and Shady Grove Orthopedic Associates (Stevens, J., controlling), when a Federal Rule answers the relevant question and is valid under the Rules Enabling Act, 28 U.S.C. § 2072, it governs in diversity; requiring an AOM would effectively impose a heightened, state-specific gatekeeping mechanism that can mandate dismissal notwithstanding compliance with federal pleading and certification rules. Applying the AOM in federal court would also risk inequitable administration by allowing a state procedural screen to defeat otherwise properly pleaded federal actions, undermining procedural fairness without a clear showing that the requirement defines the substantive elements of the claim rather than the manner and timing of filing. Because the Federal Rules already provide tools to deter nonmeritorious claims (Rule 11) and manage expert proof (Rule 26), Delaware’s AOM should be treated as displaced in federal diversity litigation.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a federal court sitting in diversity must enforce Delaware’s medical-malpractice “affidavit of merit” (AOM) pre-suit/early-suit requirement, or whether the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure displace it.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Delaware’s medical malpractice Affidavit/Certificate of Merit statute (commonly referenced as Delaware’s AOM requirement, generally codified in Title 18 of the Delaware Code governing health-care negligence actions), analyzed through the lens of the Rules Enabling Act (28 U.S.C. § 2072) and the Erie doctrine (Erie R.R. Co. v. Tompkins) as applied to the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure (especially Rules 8, 9, 11, 12, and 56).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Berk argues that Delaware’s AOM requirement is a state-law procedural screening device that conflicts with (and is therefore displaced by) the Federal Rules’ pleading and motion-to-dismiss framework; in federal court, a plaintiff should be able to commence and maintain a malpractice action by satisfying Rules 8 and 11 without an added state-law expert-affidavit gatekeeping step that can trigger dismissal based on filing mechanics rather than merits, and enforcing the AOM rule in federal court undermines uniform federal procedure and improperly heightens federal pleading in a way the Rules do not authorize.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Choy and Beebe Medical Center argue that Delaware’s AOM requirement is substantive for Erie purposes because it is tightly bound to the state-created malpractice cause of action and functions as a condition on suit designed to deter non-meritorious claims, control malpractice costs, and protect access to care; they contend there is no direct collision with any Federal Rule because the Rules govern pleading and case management generally while the AOM statute supplies an additional state-law element/condition that affects whether a Delaware malpractice claim may proceed at all, and refusing to apply it would encourage forum-shopping and create inequitable administration of the laws (state plaintiffs would face the AOM hurdle, federal diversity plaintiffs would not).
key_precedents: Shady Grove Orthopedic Assocs., P.A. v. Allstate Ins. Co.
Gasperini v. Center for Humanities, Inc.
Burlington Northern R. Co. v. Woods
Cohen v. Beneficial Industrial Loan Corp.
Byrd v. Blue Ridge Rural Electric Cooperative, Inc.
Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 8, 9, 11, 12, 56 (as the principal Rules asserted to govern the same terrain)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that Rules 8 and 11 (reinforced by 12/56) create an integrated federal regime for initiating suit and screening merit, so Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit plus mandatory dismissal operates as an extra federal pleading gate. But under Hanna and Walker v. Armco Steel, I think that frames the “question in dispute” at too high a level of generality: the Federal Rules prescribe transsubstantive pleading and certification baselines, while Delaware’s AOM is best understood as a claim-specific condition on maintaining a state-created malpractice action—something that can be applied without contradicting what the Rules require to file a complaint. Justice Kagan’s concern that construing the Rules to silently negate such state-integrated preconditions risks an unnecessary direct-collision holding is persuasive, and—consistent with Shady Grove (Stevens)—reading general Rules to displace a state condition tightly tied to the remedial design would effectively enlarge the practical availability of the state cause of action in federal court. A narrow Erie holding applying the AOM in diversity, without recharacterizing federal pleading doctrine, best serves institutional legitimacy and minimizes forum-shopping and unequal-administration concerns.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Sotomayor offer the best challenge by insisting Rules 8 and 11 (plus 12/56) comprehensively govern what must be filed and when merit is tested, so Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit is an extra federal pleading gate that “collides.” But under Hanna and Walker v. Armco Steel, that frames the “question” at too high a level of generality: the Federal Rules prescribe transsubstantive pleading and certification baselines, while Delaware defines a claim-specific prerequisite to maintaining a state-created malpractice cause of action—one that can be applied without contradicting the Rules’ text. As Justice Gorsuch and the Chief Justice note, reading Rules 8/11 to silently negate such state-integrated preconditions would risk using federal procedure to enlarge the state-law entitlement in diversity, triggering serious Rules Enabling Act concerns and the Erie forum-shopping problem. Shady Grove does not alter that conclusion because no Federal Rule is sufficiently broad, in original public meaning, to displace a state-law condition that goes to the availability of the state remedy rather than the form of a federal pleading.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that Rules 8 and 11, reinforced by 12 and 56, form an integrated federal scheme for initiating and merit-testing suits, so Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit functions as an extra pleading-stage gate with a dismissal trigger. But that frames the Hanna/Walker “same question” inquiry at too high a level of generality: the Federal Rules require a complaint and govern sanctions and merits screening, while Delaware’s statute defines a claim-specific precondition to maintaining this particular state-created malpractice action—so both can operate without textual contradiction, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize. Treating the Rules as silently forbidding any state-law condition tightly connected to the state remedial choice risks using federal procedure to enlarge the practical availability of the Delaware cause of action in diversity, raising the Rules Enabling Act concern highlighted in Shady Grove (Stevens) and aggravating Erie forum-shopping incentives. Walker’s distinction still matters here: even if a complaint may be filed under Rule 8, state law may still determine whether the plaintiff has satisfied a prerequisite to invoke the state-law remedy, and I do not see an unavoidable collision that would compel displacement.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s Walker framing is the strongest pushback, but it depends on slicing the “question” so narrowly that it obscures the statute’s operative effect: a mandatory, front-end dismissal trigger for failing to append an extra merit certification to the complaint. Rules 8 and 11 (reinforced by 12 and 56) are not just “general baselines” in the abstract; they reflect a federal choice about when and how sufficiency and merit are tested, and Delaware’s AOM overrides that timing and mechanism by converting lack of immediate expert access into a procedural forfeiture. Justice Gorsuch’s REA concern does not move me because, in practical application, the AOM is not an element of liability but an access gate that predictably falls hardest on vulnerable plaintiffs (including those proceeding with limited resources), while federal sanctions and merits screening already police frivolousness without shutting the courthouse door at filing. Under my pragmatic lens, importing this kind of affidavit trap into federal court risks inequitable administration and abridges the real availability of the federal forum, so I remain with Petitioner.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Jackson’s best point is that Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit functions as an added, dismissal-backed filing gate that looks like it regulates what must accompany a federal complaint, overlapping Rules 8 and 11. But under Hanna/Walker the relevant inquiry is whether a Federal Rule is sufficiently broad to answer the same specific question, and I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch that Rules 8/11 set transsubstantive pleading and certification baselines, while Delaware’s AOM is a claim-specific condition on maintaining a state-created malpractice action—so both can operate without direct contradiction. Shady Grove (Stevens) reinforces caution against construing general Rules to displace state provisions tightly bound up with the remedial design absent an unavoidable conflict, and here reading the Rules to preempt the AOM would risk enlarging Delaware’s malpractice remedy in federal court, triggering REA/Erie concerns. Justice Sotomayor’s timing/mechanism objection is forceful, but it depends on treating the Federal Rules as a comprehensive anti-precondition code, which I do not find in their text at the level of specificity Hanna requires.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s strongest point is textual: Rules 8 and 11 specify what is filed and what certifications attach, so Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit seems like an added federal pleading gate with a dismissal consequence. But Hanna/Walker require us to ask whether the Federal Rules are “sufficiently broad” to answer the same, more specific question Delaware answers—whether this state-created malpractice claim may be pursued absent an early expert attestation—and, as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, the Rules can operate fully (complaint, Rule 11 certification, Rule 12/56 testing) even if state law supplies a claim-specific precondition that triggers dismissal. Treating general, transsubstantive Rules 8/11 as silently negating state-integrated prerequisites risks the Rules Enabling Act problem Justice Kagan flags—federal procedure would effectively enlarge the practical availability of the state cause of action in diversity. Justice Sotomayor’s concern about “timing and mechanism” overlap does not establish an unavoidable collision on the Rules’ text; it instead shows why Erie counsels against creating a federal-court escape hatch for a state-defined condition on the remedy.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that Rules 8 and 11 (with 12/56) form an integrated federal timing-and-screening regime, so Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit effectively adds a new pleading-stage dismissal trigger. But under Hanna and Walker v. Armco Steel—as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize—the proper inquiry is whether a Federal Rule is sufficiently broad to answer the same question, and Rules 8/11 set transsubstantive pleading and certification baselines rather than purporting to forbid state-created, claim-specific preconditions attached to the availability of a malpractice remedy. Treating those general Rules as displacing the AOM would risk the Shady Grove (Stevens) Rules Enabling Act problem Justice Kagan flags by enlarging the practical availability of the state cause of action in diversity and creating an obvious forum-shopping escape hatch that Erie is meant to prevent. Walker’s distinction that Rule 3 did not answer the limitations question is not formalism here; it reflects the same principle that we should not read general Federal Rules to silently negate state-integrated prerequisites absent an unavoidable collision, which I do not see on this record.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s Walker framing is the strongest counter, but it depends on reading Rules 8 and 11 at a level of generality that drains them of their textual work: they specify what a plaintiff must file (a complaint) and the certification that attaches to that filing, with Rules 12 and 56 supplying the federal mechanisms for early termination. Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit plus mandatory dismissal functions as an additional, front-end pleading-stage condition on the sufficiency of the filed complaint to proceed—precisely the procedural domain the Federal Rules already regulate—so the “no collision” characterization understates the operative overlap. Walker is distinguishable because Rule 3 did not purport to answer when an action is commenced for limitations purposes, whereas here the Federal Rules directly address what is required to file and proceed on a complaint in federal court. Justice Gorsuch’s and Justice Kagan’s Rules Enabling Act concern assumes the AOM is bound up with the substantive right, but as written it regulates timing and paperwork at filing without altering the malpractice elements or burdens; applying the Federal Rules therefore does not abridge, enlarge, or modify Delaware substantive law within the REA’s meaning.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s Walker v. Armco framing is the strongest pushback, but it depends on characterizing Delaware’s AOM as a claim-defining “condition on the right” rather than what it functionally is: a mandatory, front-end dismissal trigger keyed to what must accompany a federal complaint to proceed, which squarely overlaps Rules 8 and 11’s integrated filing-and-certification regime (and the timing choices reflected in Rules 12, 56, and 11 sanctions). Walker is distinguishable because Rule 3 did not purport to answer the specific limitations-commencement question; here, Delaware’s statute directly dictates the sufficiency of initiating papers and imposes automatic termination for noncompliance, creating the kind of operational collision Hanna treats as dispositive. Justice Gorsuch’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s Rules Enabling Act concern assumes that ignoring the AOM would enlarge the substantive malpractice right, but under a pragmatic, consequences-focused lens the AOM does not alter elements or burdens at the merits stage—it operates as an access-and-timing gate that predictably produces forfeitures unrelated to culpability and risks the inequitable administration Justice Sotomayor highlights. Erie’s forum-shopping concern cannot justify importing state affidavit traps into federal pleading practice when the Federal Rules already provide calibrated mechanisms to deter and dispose of nonmeritorious claims without reengineering the state cause of action.

John Roberts.reasoning: The Federal Rules (including Rules 8, 9, 11, and 12) govern pleading and sanctions, but they do not clearly “answer the same question” as Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit requirement, which operates as a state-law condition on maintaining a medical-malpractice claim and screens for merit at the outset. Under Hanna and Walker v. Armco Steel, where a Federal Rule does not directly collide with a state provision bound up with the state-created right, Erie directs federal courts to apply the state rule to avoid forum shopping and inequitable administration of the laws. Even under Shady Grove (Justice Stevens’s controlling concurrence), we should construe the Rules not to displace a state requirement so closely tied to the contours of the malpractice cause of action absent an unmistakable conflict, both to respect federalism and to avoid enlarging substantive state rights through federal procedure. A narrow holding enforcing the AOM in diversity best preserves institutional legitimacy by adhering to settled Erie principles and minimizing disruption to state medical-malpractice regimes.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit requirement operates as a state-imposed condition on the maintenance of a state-created medical-malpractice cause of action, and the Federal Rules do not “answer the question in dispute” in a way that leaves no room for the statute’s operation. Rules 8, 11, 12, and 56 govern general pleading, certification, and motion practice, but they do not purport to eliminate state-law prerequisites that define when a malpractice claim may proceed, so there is no “direct collision” under Burlington Northern R. Co. v. Woods and Walker v. Armco Steel Corp. Because disregarding the AOM requirement would materially alter who can sue and would invite forum shopping and inequitable administration of the laws, Erie and Hanna counsel enforcing the Delaware rule in diversity. This conclusion respects the Rules Enabling Act’s limitation that federal rules may not abridge, enlarge, or modify substantive rights, 28 U.S.C. § 2072(b), by allowing Delaware to define the preconditions of its own tort remedy.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Under Hanna and Burlington Northern, the threshold question is whether any Federal Rule is "sufficiently broad" to control the issue and thereby create a direct collision with Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit requirement; Rules 8, 9, 11, 12, and 56 regulate pleadings and motions generally but do not purport to eliminate state-law conditions that define when a Delaware medical-negligence claim may proceed. Like the state statute in Walker v. Armco Steel, Delaware’s AOM functions as a substantive, claim-screening precondition closely tied to the state-created malpractice cause of action, and applying it in diversity avoids the forum-shopping and inequitable administration Erie sought to prevent. Shady Grove does not compel displacement absent a genuine collision, and enforcing the AOM requirement respects Delaware’s substantive policy judgment to deter non-meritorious malpractice suits and protect healthcare access. Because there is no direct Rule collision, Erie principles require the federal court to apply the Delaware AOM statute.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Delaware’s AOM requirement operates as an added, front-end gatekeeping condition that effectively heightens the showing required to initiate and keep a malpractice suit alive, colliding with the Federal Rules’ comprehensive scheme for commencing actions and testing pleadings—particularly Rules 8 and 11 (certification), enforced through Rule 12(b)(6) and later Rule 56. Under Hanna v. Plumer and the Shady Grove framework, when a Federal Rule is sufficiently broad to control the issue, it governs unless it violates the Rules Enabling Act, 28 U.S.C. § 2072(b); applying a state-law affidavit screen in federal court risks “abridg[ing]” access to the federal forum by authorizing dismissal for noncompliance with a procedural filing mechanic rather than merits. Unlike statutes that merely define elements of a claim, the AOM rule primarily regulates the manner and timing of suit and disproportionately burdens vulnerable plaintiffs (e.g., those lacking early access to experts), undermining fair access to justice without altering the substantive negligence standard. Because the Federal Rules already police frivolous malpractice filings through Rule 11 and permit early dismissal or summary judgment on the merits, Delaware’s additional affidavit requirement should be displaced in diversity.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Applying Hanna v. Plumer and Justice Stevens’s controlling concurrence in Shady Grove, the threshold question is whether any Federal Rule “answers the same question” as Delaware’s AOM requirement and thus creates a direct collision. Rules 8, 9, 11, 12, and 56 govern pleading standards, sanctions, and adjudication, but they do not purport to eliminate state-law preconditions that define when a state-created medical-malpractice claim may proceed; like Walker v. Armco Steel, the Federal Rules can operate alongside the state requirement without contradiction. Under Erie’s forum-shopping/inequitable-administration concerns and the REA’s command that Rules not “abridge, enlarge or modify any substantive right” (28 U.S.C. § 2072(b)), Delaware’s AOM statute is sufficiently bound up with the scope of the state malpractice remedy to be enforced in diversity to preserve statutory coherence and avoid a federal-court escape hatch.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: No Federal Rule squarely answers the same question as Delaware’s AOM statute—whether a plaintiff may maintain a Delaware medical-negligence claim absent an early expert attestation—because Rules 8, 11, and 12 regulate pleading sufficiency and sanctions, not state-law conditions on the availability of a particular cause of action. Under Walker v. Armco Steel and Cohen v. Beneficial Industrial Loan Corp., when the Federal Rules operate at a different level of generality and can coexist with a state condition on suit, Erie requires applying the state rule to avoid forum shopping and inequitable administration of the laws. Shady Grove displaces state law only when a Federal Rule and the state provision “answer the same question,” and this AOM requirement is better understood as an integrated state-law screen tied to the state-created malpractice claim rather than a competing federal pleading standard. Enforcing it in diversity respects state substantive choices while leaving federal procedure intact, consistent with the Rules Enabling Act’s command that federal rules not abridge, enlarge, or modify substantive rights.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under Hanna v. Plumer and Burlington Northern v. Woods, the threshold question is whether a Federal Rule is sufficiently broad to create a “direct collision” with Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit condition on maintaining a medical-malpractice action. Rules 8, 11, 12, and 56 govern pleading, sanctions, and dispositive-motion practice, but they do not answer the same question as the Delaware AOM statute—whether a plaintiff must supply early expert support as a state-law condition on proceeding with a state-created malpractice claim—so this case aligns more with Walker v. Armco Steel than Shady Grove’s Rule 23 collision. Because there is no direct conflict, Erie’s anti–forum-shopping and equal-administration principles favor enforcing Delaware’s AOM requirement in diversity to respect the State’s chosen structure for its malpractice cause of action and to preserve practical workability and uniform outcomes between state and federal court.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Under Hanna v. Plumer, the first question is whether a Federal Rule “answers the question in dispute”; here, Rules 8, 11, and 12 provide the federal standards for commencing an action and policing the sufficiency and good-faith basis of allegations, leaving no room for a state-law expert-affidavit filing prerequisite as a gatekeeping condition to maintain the suit. Delaware’s AOM requirement, insofar as it mandates dismissal for failure to file an affidavit at the outset, directly collides with that federal pleading and enforcement framework and thus yields if the Federal Rules are valid under the Rules Enabling Act, 28 U.S.C. § 2072. Applying Justice Stevens’s controlling concurrence in Shady Grove, the relevant Rules are “general rule[s] of practice and procedure” that regulate the manner and means of enforcing rights and do not abridge, enlarge, or modify any substantive right merely because they may affect outcomes. Accordingly, the Federal Rules govern in federal court and displace Delaware’s AOM mechanism in diversity cases.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Delaware’s AOM requirement functions as an added gatekeeping mechanism tied to filing and early-case screening, and in diversity it collides with the Federal Rules’ integrated scheme for initiating and testing claims—especially Rules 8 and 11 (pleading and certification), and Rules 12 and 56 (dismissal and evidentiary sufficiency). Under Hanna and Shady Grove, the question is whether the Federal Rules “answer the same question”; here, they occupy the terrain of what must be filed to commence and maintain a civil action and how merit is policed, leaving no room for a state-law affidavit prerequisite that triggers dismissal on filing mechanics rather than merits. Even under Justice Stevens’s Shady Grove concurrence (the controlling approach for assessing the Rules Enabling Act), applying a Federal Rule that governs pleading and sanctions does not “abridge, enlarge, or modify” substantive rights within 28 U.S.C. § 2072(b); it instead preserves uniform federal procedure while still allowing state substantive standards of negligence and causation to control. Enforcing the AOM in federal court would also risk inequitable administration by converting access to a federal forum into a procedural trap for the unwary, undermining procedural fairness without meaningfully advancing Delaware’s substantive standards of liability.
